# National Geographic Society Headquarters

The **National Geographic Society Headquarters** is a historic complex of buildings located at **1145 17th Street NW** and **1156 16th Street NW** in Washington, D.C., United States . The headquarters serves as the administrative center of the National Geographic Society, a scientific and educational nonprofit institution founded in 1888 . The complex consists of multiple buildings constructed in phases beginning in 1903, representing various architectural styles from the early 20th century to the present . The headquarters has achieved recognition for its sustainable design practices and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places .

## History

### Early Development (1903-1940s)

The National Geographic Society was founded on January 27, 1888, by 33 explorers and scientists who gathered at the Cosmos Club in Washington, D.C. . Initially operating from rented quarters, the society moved to its permanent headquarters in September 1903 . The original building, **Hubbard Memorial Hall**, was constructed in 1902-1903 and designed by the architectural firm Hornblower & Marshall in the neoclassical style . This building was a gift from the Hubbard and Bell families, with Gardiner Greene Hubbard serving as the society's first president and Alexander Graham Bell (his son-in-law) as his successor .

The complex expanded southward in 1931 with the addition of an administration building designed by Arthur B. Heaton . This expansion was necessitated by the growing popularity of the National Geographic Magazine and the society's expanding operations . The administration building featured architectural details including stone string courses and was constructed using traditional materials and techniques of the period .

### Mid-20th Century Expansion (1940s-1960s)

The headquarters continued to grow throughout the mid-20th century with the addition of an editors' wing in 1948 . The most significant architectural addition came in 1963-1964 with the construction of a **10-story office building** designed by internationally prominent architect Edward Durell Stone . Stone's design employed the **new formalism style**, a modern architectural approach that incorporated classical elements to create a building that "echoed the society's architectural history" while maintaining contemporary functionality .

The Stone building featured reinforced concrete structure with white marble cladding, creating a distinctive appearance on 16th Street . The building's design included a hipped roof with terracotta tiles, large arched windows, and a stone surround with a cross setting that reads "National Geographic Society" . This structure became an iconic landmark on 16th Street, recognized for its architectural significance and association with the prestigious scientific organization .

### Late 20th Century Developments (1980s)

In 1981, the headquarters underwent another major expansion with the addition of a **multifunctional building** designed by the architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) . This tiered building contained a 400-seat theater and was designed to complement the existing structures while providing modern amenities for the society's growing educational and public outreach programs .

The architectural firm worked with landscape architect James Urban to create a publicly accessible outdoor plaza adjacent to the new building . In 1984, the plaza was enhanced with the installation of **MARABAR**, a significant sculptural work commissioned by National Geographic with guidance from SOM's David Childs and designed by artist Elyn Zimmerman . This installation consisted of twelve granite boulders, some polished to a reflective surface, arranged around a rectangular reflecting pool measuring 6 by 60 feet .

### Recent History and Renovations (2000s-2020s)

In 2004, the National Geographic Society headquarters achieved a significant environmental milestone by becoming one of the first buildings to receive a "Green" certification from Global Green USA . This recognition acknowledged the society's efforts to support a sustainable and secure world through its building operations . The headquarters later became the first building to achieve a **LEED-EB (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design for Existing Buildings)** rating .

In November 2017, the society announced plans to remove the MARABAR sculpture to accommodate a plaza redesign . This decision sparked controversy in the architectural and cultural communities, with many prominent figures, including Whitney Museum director Adam Weinberg, writing letters to the D.C. Historic Preservation Review Board opposing the removal . After a year-long campaign by the Cultural Landscape Foundation, the society agreed to relocate the sculpture at its expense under Zimmerman's direction . The sculpture was dismantled in 2022 and reconfigured at American University, where it was rededicated on April 4, 2023, under the new name **Sudama** .

In 2022, the National Geographic Society headquarters received official landmark designation from the D.C. Historic Preservation Review Board . The designation covered the entire complex along M Street NW between 16th and 17th Streets, recognizing its architectural and cultural significance .

## Architecture and Design

### Architectural Styles and Buildings

The National Geographic Society Headquarters complex represents a **chronological survey of 20th-century American architecture** . The oldest building, Hubbard Memorial Hall (1902-1903), exemplifies the neoclassical style with its symmetrical facade, classical columns, and detailed stonework . The 1931 administration building by Arthur B. Heaton reflects the architectural trends of the early 20th century with its formal design and traditional materials .

The **Edward Durell Stone building** (1963-1964) represents the new formalism movement, which emerged as a reaction against the perceived austerity of pure modernism . Stone's design incorporated classical elements such as arched windows and decorative stonework while maintaining the clean lines and functionality of modern architecture . The building's white marble cladding and distinctive hipped roof with terracotta tiles create a memorable presence on 16th Street .

The **Skidmore, Owings & Merrill building** (1981) introduces a postmodernist aesthetic with its tiered design and playful use of architectural elements . The building's stepped terraces and colonnade create a dynamic relationship with the surrounding plaza and provide shaded outdoor spaces .

### Plaza and Landscape Design

The headquarters encloses an **elongated plaza** framed by buildings that reflect various 20th-century architectural styles . The plaza design minimizes the separation between pedestrian and vehicular access through a looping drop-off area bordered by a low-curbed sidewalk . A planted median runs through the center of the plaza, containing a staircase to an underground garage and featuring oak, holly, and boxelder trees .

The plaza's design creates a transition from the busy urban streetscape to a sheltered, well-shaded garden space that eventually leads to an alley exiting onto Sumner Row . The repetition of hedges along the exhibition hall's colonnade provides a sense of enclosure while maintaining visual connection to the surrounding buildings .

### MARABAR/Sudama Sculpture

The **MARABAR sculpture** (1984) was a significant work of environmental art that integrated natural and man-made elements . The installation consisted of twelve granite boulders, with three featuring highly polished and reflective surfaces that mirrored one another across the water . The boulders were strategically placed throughout the plaza's gardens, with some sinking slightly below the pavement to create the illusion that the natural elements predated the man-made construction .

The rectangular reflecting pool (6 x 60 feet) served as the sculpture's main element, creating a serene water feature that contrasted with the massive granite forms . The name "Marabar" was derived from E.M. Forster's novel *A Passage to India*, referencing the Marabar Caves described in the book .

After relocation to American University in 2023, the sculpture was renamed **Sudama**, also from Forster's novel . Zimmerman reconfigured the boulders to better fit the new site on a hill near the university's Kay Spiritual Life Center, alongside cherry trees and daffodils .

## Sustainability Features

### Environmental Achievements

The National Geographic Society has demonstrated a **long-standing commitment to sustainable design and operations** at its headquarters . In 2004, the headquarters became one of the first buildings to receive Green certification from Global Green USA, recognizing its efforts to support a sustainable and secure world . This certification was particularly significant as it came during an early period of environmental building recognition .

The headquarters achieved another milestone by becoming the **first building to achieve a LEED-EB (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design for Existing Buildings) rating** . The LEED-EB criteria covers building operations and systems upgrades in existing buildings where the majority of interior or exterior surfaces remain unchanged . The certification addressed whole-building cleaning and maintenance issues, including chemical use, and recognized the society's comprehensive approach to environmental stewardship .

### Current and Future Sustainability Initiatives

The ongoing **Museum of Exploration project** represents the society's continued commitment to sustainable design . The project is targeting **LEED Platinum certification**, the highest level of LEED recognition, when it opens in 2026 . This certification would place the National Geographic Society Headquarters among the most environmentally advanced buildings in the United States.

The new construction includes several innovative sustainability features:

* A **45,000-gallon cistern** located in the lowest parking level, designed to collect rainwater for irrigation and graywater use

* **Solar panels** that will provide approximately one-quarter of the campus's power needs 

* Recycling materials from the existing building during renovation 

* Energy-efficient lighting and mechanical systems designed to minimize environmental impact

The project team has worked to incorporate National Geographic's high standards for sustainability into every aspect of the design, from materials selection to operational systems .

## Current Facilities and Operations

### Museum of Exploration

The **National Geographic Museum of Exploration** is currently under construction and scheduled to open in 2026 . The museum represents a major transformation of the headquarters campus, uniting four historic buildings through a new pavilion and courtyard . The project is being led by general contractor HITT Contracting, with architectural design by Hickok Cole .

The new museum will feature:

* Expanded exhibition spaces showcasing engaging exhibitions, iconic photography, and world-famous artifacts

* An education center designed to be an integral part of school trips to Washington, D.C.

* A renovated theater with cutting-edge technologies and storytelling tools woven into the architecture

* A new Explorers Bar & Grill where visitors can connect and share their experiences

The museum's centerpiece is a **droplet-shaped ceiling** at the heart of the new pavilion . This ceiling design, representative of a water droplet and its ripples, allows natural light to flood the north-facing space through the Oculus skylight . The design creates a dramatic architectural statement while providing functional lighting for the exhibition spaces .

### Base Camp Concept

The National Geographic Society has reimagined its headquarters as **Base Camp**, a place where visitors can experience stunning imagery and photography, bold storytelling, and learn about rich discoveries and expeditions of the past . This concept reflects the society's mission to inspire people to care about the planet through science, exploration, education, and storytelling .

The Base Camp concept encompasses:

* Interactive exhibits that engage visitors of all ages

* Educational programs focused on the society's six key areas: Ocean, Land, Wildlife, Human Histories & Cultures, Planetary Health, and Space

* A hub for National Geographic's global community of explorers, scientists, and storytellers

* Event spaces available for private and public gatherings

### Visitor Information

The National Geographic Society Headquarters is **open to visitors** with the following hours:

* Monday: 9:00 AM - 5:00 PM

* Tuesday: 9:00 AM - 5:00 PM 

* Wednesday through Sunday: Hours vary, with some sources indicating extended hours until 7:00-10:00 PM on weekdays 

The headquarters is located at **1145 17th Street NW, Washington, DC 20036** . The complex is accessible by public transportation, including Metro rail and bus services .

## Significance and Legacy

### Cultural Importance

The National Geographic Society Headquarters has served as a **cultural and educational landmark** in Washington, D.C. for over a century . The complex has hosted numerous significant events, including memorial services honoring prominent figures such as Rosa Parks, Blanche Bruce (the first African-American U.S. Senator), and Frederick Douglass . These events highlight the headquarters' role as a venue for commemorating important figures in American history and culture .

The headquarters has also been the site of numerous groundbreaking exhibitions and educational programs that have inspired millions of visitors . The National Geographic Museum, managed by the society, offers changing photographic exhibitions that showcase the work of explorers, photographers, and scientists . These exhibitions provide a unique window into the world of exploration and discovery .

### Architectural Significance

The headquarters complex is recognized for its **architectural diversity and historical value** . The collection of buildings from different periods represents significant movements in American architecture, from neoclassical to modern to postmodernist styles . This diversity makes the complex a valuable resource for architectural education and study .

The Edward Durell Stone building, in particular, is considered a **memorable example of the new formalism style** . Stone was an early pioneer of this movement, which sought to combine modern functionality with classical aesthetic elements . By 1958, Stone was one of the best-known architects in America, and his work on the National Geographic headquarters represents a significant achievement in his career .

### Environmental Leadership

The National Geographic Society Headquarters has established itself as a **leader in sustainable building practices** . Its achievements in environmental certification, including the first LEED-EB rating and early Green certification, have influenced building standards and practices worldwide .

The society's commitment to sustainability extends beyond its own operations to influence broader building industry practices. The planned LEED Platinum certification for the Museum of Exploration project will further cement the headquarters' position as an environmental leader .

### Historic Designation

The National Geographic Society Headquarters was officially designated as a **D.C. historic landmark** in March 2022 . The designation was unanimously approved by the D.C. Historic Preservation Review Board, which accepted nominations from both the D.C. Public Library and the National Geographic Society .

The complex is also listed on the **National Register of Historic Places** . The National Register listing, with reference number SG100009025, covers both addresses at 1156 16th Street NW and 1145 17th Street NW . This dual listing at the local and national levels recognizes the headquarters' significance in American architectural and cultural history .

## Future Developments

### Museum of Exploration (2026)

The **Museum of Exploration** represents the most significant transformation of the National Geographic Society Headquarters since the 1981 addition . The project, scheduled for completion in 2026, will unite four historic buildings through innovative new construction while maintaining their historic character .

Key features of the new museum include:

* A new public entrance at 16th and M Streets NW

* A central pavilion with the distinctive droplet-shaped ceiling and Oculus skylight

* A courtyard designed to host projection shows and other outdoor events

* State-of-the-art exhibition spaces designed to showcase National Geographic's collections and expeditions

The project has been designed to maintain the campus's operations throughout construction, with the society never closing during the renovation period . This operational continuity required careful coordination and the development of over 500 detailed methods of procedure (MOPs) to ensure construction activities did not disrupt daily operations .

### Campus Modernization

The **Base Camp reimagining** represents a comprehensive modernization of the National Geographic Society Headquarters campus . This transformation goes beyond physical construction to encompass new technologies, educational approaches, and visitor experiences .

The modernization includes:

* Upgraded infrastructure to support digital technologies and multimedia presentations

* Enhanced accessibility features to accommodate visitors with disabilities

* Flexible event spaces that can adapt to various programming needs

* Improved circulation patterns to enhance the visitor experience

The project team has worked to ensure that the modernization respects the historic character of the existing buildings while introducing contemporary amenities and technologies .

> 326 AMERICAN ANTIQUARIAN SOCIETY [Oct.,

owe the honor of my election as President of the National Geographic Society simply to the fact that I am one of those who desire to further the prosecution of geographic research. I possess only the same general interest in the subject of geography that should be felt by every educated man." A few months later, early in 1889, appeared a slim little scientific brochure—^Volume I, No. i, of the National Geo-graphic Magazine. Between its paper covers of a terra cotta shade were such articles as these: "Geographic Methods in Geologic Investigation"; "The Classification of Geographic Forms by Genesis." It was earnest, serious, studious, thor-ough, but it bore little relation to the brilliantly illustrated periodical that it would some day be. After several years of irregular publication, the Board decided to issue the Maga-zine every month, beginning January i, 1896, and to make efforts to increase the circulation by placing it on the newsstands. In December, 1897, Gardiner Greene Hubbard died, and his distinguished son-in-law, Alexander Graham Bell, in-ventor of the telephone, accepted the presidency in Janu-ary, 1898. Meanwhile, the plan to popularize the Magazine 

and increase the subscriptions had failed. By the end of the year the Society was badly in debt, and the Board much discouraged. But President Bell was not disheartened. He maintained that geography was a most interesting subject and that the public would support a geographic magazine, provided the matter was presented entertainingly. The first step, he asserted, was to engage and pay a person to devote his entire time to the editorial work and to promote the membership. To his friend. Dr. Edwin A. Grosvenor,^ profes-sor of European history at Amherst College, author of two magnificently illustrated volumes on Constantinople, and later President of the United Chapters of Phi Beta Kappa,    

> ' Professor Grosvenor was elected a member of the American Antiquarian Society, 1896, on the nomination of Senator George Frisbie Hoar. 1942.] T H E NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY 327

Dr. Bell wrote on February 19, 1899, to inquire whether one of his sons would be interested to become Assistant Secretary and Managing Editor of the magazine, adding that "some bright college graduate just beginning life would probably find in this position a stepping stone to something better." Dr. Bell's proposition appealed to me more than to my brother and I accepted it. I was teaching at Englewood Academy for Boys in New Jersey. I had been engaged originally to give instruction in French, German and Latin. The principal later assigned me classes in College Algebra, Chemistry, Public Speaking, and Debating. Compared to this program, a job as Editor seemed very easy. I was born in Constantinople (Istanbul) and had spent my pre-coUege days there. My father had been professor of history in Robert College for twenty years before being called to Amherst College. My life abroad and my close association with my scholarly father had given me unusual geographic interest. I well remember my first visit, on April i, 1899, to the Society's headquarters, which was half of a small rented room on the fifth fioor of the Corcoran Building in Washington. Dr. Alexander Graham Bell took me to the office on the morning of my arrival in Washington. The little space of which I, age 23, was to assume charge was littered with old magazines, newspapers, and a few books of records, which constituted the only visible property of the Society. The treasury was empty, and had incurred a debt of nearly $2,000 by expenditure of life-membership fees to keep alive. But the Society was not so poor as it seemed, for Dr. Bell had a revolutionary idea: Why not popularize the science of geography and take it into the homes of the people . f* Why not transform the Society's 

Magazine from one of cold geographic fact, expressed in hieroglyphic terms which the layman could not understand, into a vehicle for carrying the living, breathing, human-interest truth about this great world of ours to the people . f"328 AMERICAN ANTIQUARIAN SOCIETY [Oct., 

Would not that, said Dr. Bell, be the greatest agency of all for the diffusion of geographic knowledge? To evolve a magazine that would not lower the dignity of the Society but that would win popular support was the task that was entrusted to me. Dr. Bell personally for five years con-tributed my salary as Assistant Editor and Editor, making a total gift of $6,900 to the Society for this purpose. The Society was so poor that it could employ no clerical assist-ance, and for a time I was even obliged to address the

When Alexander Graham Bell asked me to take charge of the National Geographic Magazine, April i, 1899, the Society's membership was so small that I could carry the entire edition of one month on my back. The National Geographic maps, concise, convenient in size, accurate, represent many years of research in computa-tions, in compiling of data, and in devising new methods for delineating the world's surface so that the maximum of information can be given distinctly. They tap surveys, data, and exploration notes of decades, accumulated by the Society's expeditions, staff writers, and photographers and correspondents abroad; also reports garnered from foreign governments and geographic societies all over the world, and correspondence carefully collated and classified. Maps are the shorthand of geography, and special pro-cesses make it possible to concentrate into those issued by the Society a maximum of material without crowding and with a clarity of lettering that has been the envy of cartog-raphers in other parts of the world. By a specially devised 1942.] T H E NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOICETY 361 

technique place names are photographed onto the map instead of being printed. Paper and inks are carefully se-lected to insure the perfection and durability of the finished product. First printings of each map run up to a million and a half copies. The National Geographic modern series comprises 22 big ten-color maps with 120,000 place names. The maps and accompanying indexes constitute a handy atlas of the world and a gazetteer of geographic information unequaled for scope, accuracy, legibility, and timeliness. The Saturday Review of Literature lists them as "the best general layman's series of maps." In A Key to Maps, Brigadier H. S. L. Winterbotham, C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., sometime Director-General of the British Ordnance Survey, writes: "In this matter of the general map the members of the National Geographic Society of the United States are lucky, for they, and apparently only they, can get copies of the excellent series produced by that body." This map program the National Geographic Society has carried on for many years as an important altruistic public service. The membership fees have paid for it as well as for 

theNational Geographic Magazine and the many explorations and other researches of the Society. From 1915 to 1940 this cartographic work was directed by Albert H. Bumstead, whose untimely death on January 9, 1940, was a sad loss to the Society and to science. It was Mr. Bumstead who invented the sun-compass which Ad-miral Byrd used on his polar fiights. "Without it," Byrd said, "we could not have reached the Pole." His able assistant, Mr. James M. Darley, succeeded Mr. Bumstead as Chief Cartographer. Men of great ability and national prominence have served on the Board of Trustees. They have given generously of time and valuable experience to help the Society. Especially 362 AMERICAN ANTIQUARIAN SOCIETY [Oct., 

and gratefully remembered are: John Joy Edson, Treasurer, 1901-1934; Charles J. Bell, brother-in-law and first cousin of Alexander Graham Bell, Chairman of the Finance Com-mittee, 1900-1929; Frederick V. Coville, Chairman of the Research Committee, 1920-1937; Robert V. Fleming, Treas-urer, 1934-; Elisha Hanson, General Counsel, 1931-; Henry White; General John J. Pershing; Chief Justice Charles Evans Hughes; Calvin Coolidge; Admiral Robert E. Peary; Stephen T. Mather; Daniel C. Gilman; Charles G. Dawes; Theodore W. Noyes; Charles F. Kettering; David Fairchild; George Shiras, 3d; Grove Karl Gilbert (President 1904); Walter S. Gifïord; my twin brother, Edwin P. Grosvenor, General Counsel, 1920-1930; Lyman J. Briggs and Alexander Wetmore, Chairman and Vice-chairman of the Research Committee, 1937-; O. P. Austin; Admiral William V. Pratt, U.S. Navy; Admiral L. 0. Colbert; Leroy A. Lincoln; George Otis Smith; General John M. Wilson, U.S. Army; Admiral C. M. Chester,U.S. Navy; Admiral J. E. Pillsbury (President 1919); Rudolph Kauffman; George R. Putnam; Ernest E. Norris; Lloyd Wilson; Admiral Emory S. Land, U.S. Navy; Juan T. Trippe, and General H. H. Arnold. Thirty-five colleges and universities are represented on the editorial, executive and research staff. Fifty-eight of the staff are now in the Army and Navy. Of the 650 employees,more than 100 have served the Society at least 20 years. Some are mentioned on preceding pages. Special credit is also due to the Society's gifted and industrious editors and staff writers, J. R. Hildebrand, Frederick Simpich, Melville Bell Grosvenor (the fourth generation of his family privileged to serve the Society), McFall Kerbey, Maynard Owen Williams, Robert Moore, Leonard C. Roy, Leo A. Borah, Gerard F. Hubbard, Inez B. Ryan, William Joseph Showalter and Ralph A. Graves. Their united enthusiasm, devotion and skill built the National Geographic Society.

Notice.

SUMMARY:
========

The National Park Service is soliciting electronic comments on the significance of properties nominated before April 22, 2023, for listing or related actions in the National Register of Historic Places.

DATES:
======

Comments should be submitted electronically by May 19, 2023.

ADDRESSES:
==========

Comments are encouraged to be submitted electronically to _[National\_Register\_Submissions@nps.gov](mailto:National\_Register\_Submissions@nps.gov)_ with the subject line “Public Comment on <property or proposed district name, (County) State>.” If you have no access to email, you may send them via U.S. Postal Service and all other carriers to the National Register of Historic Places, National Park Service, 1849 C Street NW, MS 7228, Washington, DC 20240.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
================================

Sherry A. Frear, Chief, National Register of Historic Places/National Historic Landmarks Program, 1849 C Street NW, MS 7228, Washington, DC 20240, _[sherry\_frear@nps.gov](mailto:sherry\_frear@nps.gov),_ 202-913-3763.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
==========================

The properties listed in this notice are being considered for listing or related actions in the National Register of Historic Places. Nominations for their consideration were received by the National Park Service before April 22, 2023. Pursuant to section 60.13 of [36 CFR part 60](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-36/part-60), comments are being accepted concerning the significance of the nominated properties under the National Register criteria for evaluation.

Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment—including your personal identifying information—may be made publicly available at any time. While you can ask us in your comment to withhold your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.

**English:** The [National Geographic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society "en:National Geographic Society") headquarters located at 1156 16th Street NW in Washington, D.C. The neoclassical original building, **Hubbard Memorial Hall**, was constructed in 1902 and designed by [Hornblower & Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornblower_%26_Marshall "en:Hornblower & Marshall"). A Renaissance Revival addition designed by [Arthur B. Heaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_B._Heaton "en:Arthur B. Heaton") was built in 1913. Heaton also designed the adjoining neoclassical Administration Building that was completed in 1932. Both buildings are contributing properties to the [Sixteenth Street Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixteenth_Street_Historic_District "en:Sixteenth Street Historic District").

National Geographic Museum
==========================

_**open**_ Daily: 10am-6pm$

**Share:**0 0 0

[Email](mailto:?subject=Information%20from%20Old%20Town%20Trolley&body=Hello,%20Here%20is%20some%20information%20from%20Old%20Town%20Trolley%20Tours%20regarding%20National%20Geographic%20Museum%20-%20www.trolleytours.com%2Fwashington-dc%2Fnational-geographic-museum)[Print](https://www.trolleytours.com/washington-dc/national-geographic-museum#)

![Image 13: national geographic museum in Washington DC](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/national-geographic-museum-480x270.jpg)

**Note: The National Geographic Museum is temporarily closed as they reimagine their Base Camp experience. The Museum Store will remain open.**

Just like the highly acclaimed magazine, the National Geographic Museum offers a stunning representation of the world we live in within its collection of exhibits, both permanent and changing. Adults and children will be intrigued by the colorful, interactive and extraordinary displays. From sculptures created entirely out of garbage to live frogs of every color in their natural habitats, there’s always something fascinating happening at the National Geographic Museum.

*   ![Image 14: Admissions](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/themes/oldtowntrolley/images/icon-admissions.png) Admissions 
*   ![Image 15: Shopping](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/themes/oldtowntrolley/images/icon-shopping.png) Shopping 
*   ![Image 16: Dining](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/themes/oldtowntrolley/images/icon-dinning.png) Dining 
*   ![Image 17: Entertainment](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/themes/oldtowntrolley/images/icon-entertainment.png) Entertainment 
*   ![Image 18: Restrooms](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/themes/oldtowntrolley/images/icon-restrooms.png) Restrooms 

The National Geographic Society was established in January 1888 when a group of 33 explorers and scientists met in the private Cosmos Club on [Lafayette Square](https://www.trolleytours.com/washington-dc/lafayette-park). Their goal was to create an organization that would foster the increase and dissemination of geographic knowledge. The society’s first president was Gardiner Greene Hubbard, father-in-law of Alexander Graham Bell who would succeed him nine years later. Along with his son-in-law Gilbert Grosvenor, the famed inventor devised the successful membership program and the first use of photographs as a way to illustrate stories in the magazine. The society is one of the world’s largest non-profit scientific and educational organizations. It has expanded its scope to include archaeology, natural science, and environmental conservation. In addition to studying and documenting world cultures and history, the society sponsors and funds scientific research and exploration.

The National Geographic magazine was first published nine months after the society was founded. There are 12 monthly issues. Article subjects include current events, culture, and world history as well as popular science and geography. The magazine began using its famous trademarked yellow border in 1910. It is published in 40 languages around the world with a circulation of just under seven million. More than 60 million people read an issue each month. The society also publishes National Geographic Explorer and National Geographic Kids to help classroom education and encourage early learning. Society television programs have aired on various networks since 1964. The NatGeo Channel was launched in 1997. The society also has a website that features additional content.

> The National Geographic Society Museum

Located on the first floor of the organization’s headquarters in Washington, D.C., the museum’s two large galleries display a variety of permanent and changing exhibitions that enable visitors to explore and discover the natural world. It features a wide range of interactive displays and stunning photo collections that are suitable for patrons of all ages. Celebrating the society’s more than 125-year history, the museum provides a glimpse into the unique perspective of renowned scientists, historians, photographers, and explorers. See how these individuals study and chronicle places and events that inspire people to care about the planet. Exhibits, which take approximately an hour to view, are related to culture, history, society and [natural history](https://www.trolleytours.com/washington-dc/smithsonian-museum-natural-history). In addition to photographs and memorabilia, the exhibits feature live animals, ancient artifacts, 3D models and captivating films. Guided tours are available.

> Know Before You Go

The National Geographic Museum is open daily from 10 a.m. until 6 p.m. It is closed Thanksgiving and Christmas. The ticket booth is located at the 17th street entrance. Discounts to the general admission price are available to seniors, students and military personnel. Exhibits in the M street lobby can be viewed free of charge. The museum is located near the Farragut North stop on the Metro Red line. You can also use the Farragut West stop on the Blue, Orange, and Silver lines. Metered street parking is located on 16th, 17th, and M streets.

> Attractions Nearby

Scott Circle Park contains an equestrian statue of Lieutenant General Winfield Scott who served as the Commanding General of the Army for 20 years, the Daniel Webster Memorial and the Samuel Hahnemann Monument. The Webster Memorial includes a larger-than-life-size bronze statue of the famed political leader and the Classical Revival-style Hahnemann Monument honors the founder of homeopathy.

![Image 19: national archives](https://www.trolleytours.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/stop-3-national-archives-300x200.jpg)[The Charles Sumner School Museum and Archives](https://www.trolleytours.com/washington-dc/charles-sumner-museum) were built in 1872. It is named in honor of U.S. Senator Charles Sumner, an abolitionist and staunch civil rights activist featured in the acclaimed Steven Spielberg film “Lincoln.” The building was used to educate African-American teachers after the Civil War and as the headquarters for the segregated school district. In addition to artifacts and memorabilia, the small museum hosts rotating art exhibits and the DC Women’s Hall of Fame.

Construction on the Romanesque Revival-style Cathedral of St. Matthew the Apostle began in 1893. The interior of the historic red brick, sandstone, and terracotta edifice features marble and semi-precious stone architectural details. Each year, the church is the setting for the famous Red Mass on the day before the start of the new [Supreme Court](https://www.trolleytours.com/washington-dc/us-supreme-court) term.

Built in 1886, the historic Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church is the oldest continuously Black-owned property within the city’s original 10-square mile area. It was the setting for memorial services honoring Rosa Parks, Blanche Bruce, the first African-American U.S. Senator, and Frederick Douglass. The building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

La **National Geographic Society** (**NGS**) è una organizzazione [scientifica](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scienza "Scienza") ed educativa [statunitense](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stati_Uniti "Stati Uniti") tra le più grandi al mondo, con sede in [Washington](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington "Washington") e [senza scopi di lucro](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organizzazione_non_a_scopo_di_lucro "Organizzazione non a scopo di lucro"). Gli interessi comprendono svariate discipline, quali la [geografia](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geografia "Geografia"), l'[archeologia](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeologia "Archeologia") e le [scienze naturali](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scienze_naturali "Scienze naturali"), ma anche la cura per la conservazione dell'[ambiente naturale](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambiente_naturale "Ambiente naturale") e dei patrimoni storici, e la divulgazione dello studio circa le civiltà umane e la loro storia.

[![Image 5: Studio portrait of a woman in an ornate traditional dress and veil against a bright white wall](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Dancer_of_the_Cafes_NGM-v31-p269.jpg/250px-Dancer_of_the_Cafes_NGM-v31-p269.jpg)](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dancer_of_the_Cafes_NGM-v31-p269.jpg)

_A dancer of the cafes_, Algeria, 1917. Fotografia tratta da un numero del _National Geographic Magazine_

Il 13 gennaio 1888 un gruppo di 33 persone composto da scienziati ed esploratori si riunì al _Cosmos Club_, un [club privato](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_privato "Club privato") situato in [Lafayette Square](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/President's_Park?action=edit&redlink=1 "President's Park (la pagina non esiste)") a [Washington](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington "Washington"), con l'obiettivo di creare una società «per migliorare e diffondere le conoscenze geografiche». Dopo aver stabilito un regolamento e un piano per l'organizzazione, il 27 gennaio venne fondata la _National Geographic Society_.

[Gardiner Greene Hubbard](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardiner_Greene_Hubbard "Gardiner Greene Hubbard") ne fu il primo presidente e nel 1897, dopo la sua morte, gli succedette alla guida il genero, [Alexander Graham Bell](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Graham_Bell "Alexander Graham Bell"). La prima donna eletta nel consiglio di amministrazione fu [Eliza Scidmore](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliza_Scidmore "Eliza Scidmore").

Il genero di Bell, [Gilbert Hovey Grosvenor](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Hovey_Grosvenor?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gilbert Hovey Grosvenor (la pagina non esiste)"), fu nominato editore a tempo pieno del _National Geographic Magazine_ e servì l'organizzazione per 55 anni; altri membri della famiglia Grosvenor ricoprirono importanti ruoli nella società.

Bell e suo genero elaborarono il concetto di [marketing](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing "Marketing") all'interno della società ed incoraggiarono un uso sempre più ampio di materiale fotografico a corredo dei [reportage](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reportage "Reportage").

Il presidente dell'organizzazione è [Gilbert Melville Grosvenor](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Melville_Grosvenor?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gilbert Melville Grosvenor (la pagina non esiste)"), che ha ricevuto nel 2005 la [Medaglia presidenziale della libertà](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medaglia_presidenziale_della_libert%C3%A0 "Medaglia presidenziale della libertà") per la sua guida della società all'educazione geografica.

Nel 2004 il quartier generale della _NGS_ a Washington fu una delle prime costruzioni a ricevere la certificazione _Green_[[1]](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society#cite_note-1) dalla Global Green USA.[[2]](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society#cite_note-2) Nell'ottobre del 2006 la società National Geographic ha ottenuto il [Premio Principe delle Asturie](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premio_Principe_delle_Asturie "Premio Principe delle Asturie") di [Oviedo](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oviedo "Oviedo"), in Spagna, nel campo della Comunicazione e umanistica.

L'obiettivo storico della National Geographic Society è da sempre quello di «_incrementare e diffondere la conoscenza geografica e allo stesso tempo di promuovere la protezione della cultura dell'umanità, della storia e delle risorse naturali_».[[3]](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society#cite_note-3) Il suo stesso [presidente e direttore generale](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") dal marzo 1998, [John M. Fahey, Jr.](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Fahey?action=edit&redlink=1 "John M. Fahey (la pagina non esiste)"), afferma che lo scopo della _NGS_ è soprattutto stimolare le persone a prendersi cura del proprio pianeta.

La società è gestita da ventitré membri del consiglio degli amministratori fiduciari, costituito da un gruppo di esimi educatori, uomini d'affari, importanti funzionari governativi e [conservazionisti](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservazionismo "Conservazionismo"). L'organizzazione sponsorizza e promuove l'esplorazione e la ricerca scientifica, e pubblica inoltre una sua rivista, il _[National Geographic Magazine](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Geographic\_Magazine "National Geographic Magazine")_, e diverse altre riviste, libri, pubblicazioni scolastiche, mappe, filmati e inserti web in numerose lingue e paesi di tutto il mondo. La _NGS_ ha un fondamento educativo attraverso il quale dona concessioni alle organizzazioni a fine didattico con lo scopo di valorizzare l'educazione geografica.[[4]](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society#cite_note-ngef-4) Lo stesso Comitato per la Ricerca e l'Esplorazione ha offerto concessioni per la ricerca scientifica, e recentemente le ha conferito la sua nove millesima donazione; le varie proprietà comprendono una fascia di 360 milioni di persone al mese in tutto il mondo.[[5]](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society#cite_note-statedept-5)

La National Geographic Society mantiene un museo aperto al pubblico nella propria sede di Washington, ed ha aiutato la sponsorizzazione di importanti esposizioni itineranti come la _[King Tut](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/King\_Tut\_(mostra)?action=edit&redlink=1 "King Tut (mostra) (la pagina non esiste)")_, mostra che ha esposto meravigliosi reperti provenienti dalla tomba del giovane [faraone](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faraone "Faraone")[Tutankhamon](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutankhamon "Tutankhamon") e che coinvolse numerose città americane, concludendosi con l'esposizione al _[Franklin Institute](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin\_Institute "Franklin Institute")_ di [Filadelfia](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filadelfia "Filadelfia"). La mostra _King Tut_ è attualmente presente a Londra. La National Geographic Society ha inoltre contribuito alla mostra dei «Tesori culturali dell'[Afghanistan](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan")», inaugurata nel maggio [2008](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008 "2008") alla [National Gallery of Art](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Art "National Gallery of Art") di Washington, e spostatasi nei seguenti diciotto mesi all'[Houston Museum of Fine Arts](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Museum_of_Fine_Arts "Houston Museum of Fine Arts"), all'[Asian Art Museum](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Art_Museum?action=edit&redlink=1 "Asian Art Museum (la pagina non esiste)") di [San Francisco](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), e infine al [Metropolitan Museum](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum "Metropolitan Museum") di [New York](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York "New York").

Il National Geographic Explorer visita l'Antartide

Nel corso degli anni la Società ha sponsorizzato molte spedizioni e progetti di ricerca in tutto il mondo:

*   [Robert Peary](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Peary "Robert Peary") e [Matthew Henson](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Henson "Matthew Henson") - Spedizione al [Polo nord](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo_nord "Polo nord") (1905)
*   [Hiram Bingham](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiram_Bingham_III "Hiram Bingham III") - Scavi a [Machu Picchu](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu "Machu Picchu") (1915)
*   [Robert F. Griggs](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F_Griggs?action=edit&redlink=1 "Robert F Griggs (la pagina non esiste)") - [Valle dei Diecimila Fumi](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valle_dei_Diecimila_Fumi "Valle dei Diecimila Fumi") (1916)
*   [Robert Bartlett](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bartlett "Robert Bartlett") - Esplorazioni [artiche](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artide "Artide") (1925-45)
*   [Richard E. Byrd](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_E._Byrd "Richard E. Byrd") - Primo volo al di sopra del [Polo sud](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo_sud "Polo sud") (1929)
*   [Jacques-Yves Cousteau](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Yves_Cousteau "Jacques-Yves Cousteau") - Esplorazioni sottomarine
*   [Codice Tchacos](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codice_Tchacos "Codice Tchacos") - Conservazione e traduzione dell'unica copia conosciuta del [Vangelo di Giuda](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vangelo_di_Giuda "Vangelo di Giuda")
*   [Ian Baker](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Baker?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ian Baker (la pagina non esiste)") - Scoperta delle cascate nascoste del fiume [Yarlung Tsangpo](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarlung_Tsangpo "Yarlung Tsangpo") nel [Tsangpo Gorge](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsangpo_Gorge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tsangpo Gorge (la pagina non esiste)") (Yarlung Zangbo Grand Canyon), [Tibet](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet")
*   [Robert Ballard](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Ballard "Robert Ballard") - Scoperta dei relitti sottomarini del [RMS _Titanic_](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Titanic "RMS Titanic") (1985) e del [PT-109](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/PT-109 "PT-109") di [John F. Kennedy](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") (2002)
*   [George Bass](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Bass_(archeologo)?action=edit&redlink=1 "George Bass (archeologo) (la pagina non esiste)") - [Archeologia sottomarina](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeologia_sottomarina?action=edit&redlink=1 "Archeologia sottomarina (la pagina non esiste)")
*   [Lee Berger](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Berger?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lee Berger (la pagina non esiste)") - Le più antiche impronte mai scoperte lasciate nel terreno da esseri umani moderni
*   [Mike Fay](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Michael_Fay "J. Michael Fay") - [MegaTransect](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/MegaTransect?action=edit&redlink=1 "MegaTransect (la pagina non esiste)") (1999) e [MegaFlyover](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/MegaFlyover?action=edit&redlink=1 "MegaFlyover (la pagina non esiste)") (2004) in Africa
*   [Dian Fossey](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dian_Fossey "Dian Fossey") - [Gorilla di montagna](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorilla_di_montagna "Gorilla di montagna")
*   [Birutė Galdikas](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birut%C4%97_Galdikas "Birutė Galdikas") - [Oranghi](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orango "Orango")
*   [Jane Goodall](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Goodall "Jane Goodall") - [Scimpanzé](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scimpanz%C3%A9 "Scimpanzé")
*   [Heather Halstead](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heather_Halstead?action=edit&redlink=1 "Heather Halstead (la pagina non esiste)") - Circumnavigazione del mondo di _Reach the World_
*   [Louis](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Leakey "Louis Leakey") e [Mary Leakey](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Leakey "Mary Leakey") - Scoperta del Zinjanthropus (1,75 milioni di anni)
*   [Gustavus McLeod](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavus_McLeod?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gustavus McLeod (la pagina non esiste)") - Primo volo fino al [Polo nord](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo_nord "Polo nord") su un aereo con abitacolo aperto
*   [Paul Sereno](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Sereno "Paul Sereno") - [Dinosauri](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosauro "Dinosauro")

*   [Spencer Wells](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Wells?action=edit&redlink=1 "Spencer Wells (la pagina non esiste)") - [The Genographic Project](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Genographic_Project?action=edit&redlink=1 "The Genographic Project (la pagina non esiste)")
*   [Xu Xing](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Xing_(paleontologo) "Xu Xing (paleontologo)") - Scoperta di dinosauri fossili dotati di penne in [Cina](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cina "Cina")

La Società sostiene inoltre molti progetti sociali tra cui l'AINA: un'organizzazione con base a [Kabul](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabul "Kabul") che si dedica allo sviluppo del giornalismo locale, fondata da [Reza Deghati](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reza_Deghati "Reza Deghati"), uno dei più famosi fotografi della Società.

[![Image 40: The Hubbard Medal is a gold medal awarded by the National Geographic Society for distinction in exploration, discovery, and research](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Hubbard_Gold_Medal%2C_Anne_Morrow_Lindbergh.JPG/250px-Hubbard_Gold_Medal%2C_Anne_Morrow_Lindbergh.JPG)](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hubbard_Gold_Medal,_Anne_Morrow_Lindbergh.JPG)

La medaglia personalizzata di [Anne Morrow Lindbergh](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Morrow_Lindbergh "Anne Morrow Lindbergh") che mostra la sua rotta di volo.

La [Medaglia Hubbard](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medaglia_Hubbard?action=edit&redlink=1 "Medaglia Hubbard (la pagina non esiste)") è un premio della National Geographic Society per chi si è distinto nell'esplorazione, nelle scoperte e nella ricerca. La medaglia prende il nome da [Gardiner Greene Hubbard](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardiner_Greene_Hubbard "Gardiner Greene Hubbard"), il primo presidente della Società. Al 2018 è stata conferita 44 volte, di cui la più recente a Peter H. Raven, botanico.

Rivista pubblicata dal settembre 1975, è una versione per ragazzi della più famosa _[National Geographic Magazine](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Geographic\_Magazine "National Geographic Magazine")_[[8]](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic_Society#cite_note-8).
